title: Nutrition DDS · TUMS · undated 40-item photographed paper
originalFilename: Final exam of nutrition of DDS - TUMS.pdf
scopeNote: Undated DDS paper; source pages are out of order (PDF p3 contains Q37–40). Handwritten selections are student/source marks, not an authenticated official answer key. All editorial keys are independently assessed; two defective items remain ungraded. Public derivative removes a student name from p1; Downloads original is untouched.

questions.prompt: The primary sugar in the fruit is:
questions.explanation: Fructose is traditionally called fruit sugar. Actual proportions of fructose, glucose and sucrose vary among fruits; the item tests the conventional name, not every fruit composition.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 57–58 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Source wording is generalized.

questions.prompt: Raffinose which is found in sugar beets is a
questions.explanation: Raffinose contains galactose, glucose and fructose: three monosaccharide residues. It is an oligosaccharide and specifically a trisaccharide.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin deficiency is the most significant cause of blindness?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia and is an important preventable cause of childhood blindness. The stem concerns vitamin-deficiency blindness, not the leading cause of all blindness.
questions.note: Scope: deficiency-related preventable blindness.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin is used to absorb calcium and phosphorus to create bone?
questions.explanation: Active vitamin D supports intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and normal mineralization.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin is the most important lipid soluble antioxidant in the cell?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E, particularly alpha-tocopherol, protects membrane lipids against oxidation.

questions.prompt: Hemorrhagic disease in the newborn is treated by intramuscularly administration of:
questions.explanation: The appropriate vitamin form is K1 (phytonadione/phylloquinone), not menadione. The photographed C mark is incorrect. Established bleeding requires urgent clinical assessment and treatment; this item identifies the vitamin form, not a complete treatment protocol.
questions.note: Handwritten C is retained as a source mark, not an official key.

questions.prompt: Tryptophan can be converted to which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan can contribute to niacin (vitamin B3) synthesis; this relationship is expressed in niacin equivalents.

questions.prompt: A triacylglycerol molecule includes all of the following elements, except:
questions.explanation: Triacylglycerols contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but not nitrogen. Some other lipids, including phosphatidylcholine, do contain nitrogen.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 83–89 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Repaired to specify triacylglycerol rather than falsely excluding nitrogen from every lipid.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin is not fat soluble?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is water-soluble; vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

questions.prompt: Which of the following contains cholesterol?
questions.explanation: Fish is an animal food and supplies cholesterol; unfortified plant foods contain no dietary cholesterol.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 87–94 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: Which of the following options is one of the most important elements of trace minerals?
questions.explanation: Iron is a trace mineral. Calcium, magnesium and sodium are classified as major minerals.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 245–249, 259–264 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: ........ is the most abundant mineral in the body with ........ of total body mineral.
questions.explanation: Calcium is the most abundant body mineral, conventionally approximately 40% of total body mineral mass; 39% is the closest source option. This is not 39% of body weight.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 254–257 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Approximate textbook fraction, not a fixed individual measurement. Source options are numbered 1–4.

questions.prompt: Factor hindering calcium absorption is ........ .
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency reduces efficient intestinal calcium absorption. Calcitriol facilitates absorption; fractional absorption can rise at lower intakes.

questions.prompt: Which one is the strongest source of calcium?
questions.explanation: Dairy products are the conventional best general category among these options. Calcium content and absorption depend on the specific food; fish with edible bones and fortified coconut beverages can also be rich sources.
questions.note: Assumes ordinary unfortified foods and fish without edible bones; not a universal ranking of every product.

questions.prompt: Two-thirds of the iron in your body is found in ........ .
questions.explanation: Most body iron is present in hemoglobin, conventionally about two-thirds. The precise fraction varies with physiological state.

questions.prompt: Which of the following mineral is used for cavity prevention?
questions.explanation: Fluoride helps prevent dental caries by supporting remineralization and limiting demineralization.

questions.prompt: Which of the following has a highest contribution to weight gain during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The fetus and maternal fat stores are both large contributors. Their relative amounts vary; the local textbook example shows 7 lb for the infant and 7 lb for necessary maternal fat alone, with additional supporting muscle. Thus the combined fat-and-muscle category prevents a defensible unique answer.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 319–320, Figure 11-6 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Unresolved source wording: handwritten D cannot establish a universally correct maximum. Kept ungraded rather than silently changing the concept.

questions.prompt: What percentage of nitrogen is contained in protein?
questions.explanation: Dietary protein contains about 16% nitrogen on average; the conventional conversion is nitrogen × 6.25 = protein.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 109–116 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: ........ is associated with edema, malnutrition and loss of appetite.
questions.explanation: Edema is a defining clinical feature of kwashiorkor/severe edematous malnutrition; pure marasmus classically features severe wasting without nutritional edema.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–118, 426 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) decreases with?
options: It is stable all the time
questions.explanation: BMR tends to decrease with ageing, particularly with loss of lean tissue. Pregnancy and fever/infection commonly increase energy demands.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 166–169 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: In a child, bone pain, muscle weakness and dental problems accompany defective mineralization of growing bones from vitamin D deficiency. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D-deficiency rickets causes defective mineralization in children and can produce bone pain, muscle weakness and dental abnormalities. The original nonspecific symptoms also overlap with scurvy.
questions.note: The repaired stem supplies the missing age/mineralization context to distinguish rickets from scurvy.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin is likely to become a teratogen in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Excess preformed vitamin A/retinoids can cause congenital abnormalities. This does not imply dietary beta-carotene has the same teratogenic risk.

questions.prompt: Dietary fat ........
options: Increases gastric secretion with no effect on gastric emptying
Decreases gastric secretion and slows gastric emptying
Decreases gastric secretion and increases gastric emptying
Increases gastric secretion and inhibits pancreatic and biliary flow
questions.explanation: Fat reaching the small intestine generates feedback, including CCK-mediated inhibition of gastric emptying, and promotes pancreatic/biliary responses. B is the intended best description.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 133–141 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Both B and C have marks on the photograph; no unambiguous provided key.

questions.prompt: Which fats are viewed as being healthier than other fatty acids used for cooking and eating?
questions.explanation: Both mono- and polyunsaturated fats are generally preferred when replacing saturated or trans fats. The original wording does not distinguish the two unsaturated classes, so either A or B is accepted.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 83–99 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Multiple defensible answers; the source marked B.

questions.prompt: Which option describes the dominant fatty-acid class in coconut oil?
questions.explanation: Coconut oil is predominantly saturated fat. It also has relatively little stearic acid, so the unrepaired broad wording makes D true as well.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 83–86 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Repaired to ask the dominant fatty-acid class rather than any true compositional feature.

questions.prompt: In which age one should take high levels of calcium to increase the highest body calcium mass?
questions.explanation: Childhood and adolescence are crucial for skeletal mineral acquisition. Adequate calcium, vitamin D and activity support peak bone mass; the question is not a recommendation for excessive supplementation.
questions.note: Peak bone mass is reached later in early adulthood; A is the best formative interval among these broad choices.

questions.prompt: Which symptom may accompany dehydration in pregnancy and improve with rest and drinking water?
options: Transient uterine irritability or Braxton Hicks contractions
questions.explanation: Dehydration may be associated with uterine irritability/Braxton Hicks contractions. Such contractions are not proof of true preterm labor, and persistent symptoms need clinical assessment. The original option overstates a direct causal link to early labor.
questions.note: Repaired option D to avoid teaching that inadequate drinking necessarily causes preterm labor.

questions.prompt: Which one has the highest total amount of glycogen in the body?
questions.explanation: The total skeletal-muscle glycogen store exceeds the liver store because total muscle mass is much greater. Liver has a higher glycogen concentration per gram. The photographed liver mark confuses concentration with whole-body amount.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 59–63 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Source B corrected to C; preserve the distinction between concentration and total quantity.

questions.prompt: At which stage of pregnancy there is the highest need of calorie requirement per day?
questions.explanation: Additional energy needs are highest in the third trimester in conventional singleton-pregnancy recommendations. Individual requirements depend on prepregnancy status and activity.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 314–316 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: Burning fat to compensate low carbohydrate intake during pregnancy is more dangerous for?
questions.explanation: The intended marked answer is fetal brain cells, referring to concern about maternal ketosis. The stem conflates ordinary fat oxidation, nutritional ketosis and pathological ketoacidosis; a universal fetal-neurotoxicity claim is not established by this wording.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 314–316 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Unresolved: cannot treat normal fat oxidation as proven fetal brain injury. Preserved for source review, not scored.

questions.prompt: Cretinism is caused by ........ deficiency.
questions.explanation: Severe iodine deficiency during fetal/early brain development can cause congenital iodine-deficiency syndrome, historically termed cretinism.
questions.note: Historical terminology is retained in the source stem.

questions.prompt: Increased incidence of hip fracture in elderly could be the result of
options: Too much consumption of vitamin A
Too much consumption of vitamin E
questions.explanation: Excess preformed vitamin A has been associated with adverse skeletal effects. Low protein intake can also contribute to frailty and fracture risk. The broadly worded question therefore accepts B and D; neither is a sufficient diagnosis by itself.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 384–395 (PDF counter).
questions.note: Multiple plausible risk factors; source B is not uniquely entailed.

questions.prompt: What is the energy required to digest, absorb, and metabolize nutrients?
questions.explanation: The thermic effect of food is the energy cost of processing a meal, including digestion, absorption and metabolism.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 166–168 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: Which listed food supplies iron in non-heme form without supplying heme iron?
questions.explanation: Legumes supply non-heme iron only. Animal foods contain non-heme iron as well as heme iron, so specifying absence of heme makes the distinction fair.
questions.note: Original wording could include animal foods too; the study stem clarifies exclusively non-heme.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which one is the source of non-heme iron?

questions.prompt: According to BMI which one is correct?
options: In healthy weight person BMI is 16.5–25
In extreme obesity BMI is over 38
questions.explanation: For standard adult BMI categories, overweight is 25.0–29.9 kg/m². Healthy weight starts at 18.5; obesity starts at 30 and class III at 40. BMI has clinical limitations and is not used identically in children/pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Which has the shortest oral retention when swallowed promptly once, compared with the sticky foods listed, rather than repeatedly sipped?
questions.explanation: A drink swallowed promptly generally has less oral retention than sticky carbohydrate foods. Sugary drinks remain cariogenic, especially when repeatedly sipped, and acidic drinks can erode enamel. The original stem lacks frequency/retention context.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF p. 64, Sugar and Dental Caries (PDF counter).
questions.note: Repaired to test retention, not to label sweet drinks safe for teeth.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which carbohydrate consumption affects less on the progression of carious lesion?

questions.prompt: Immediately after consuming acidic foods and beverages, which is wrong for the health of the teeth?
questions.explanation: Immediate brushing after an acidic exposure can abrade acid-softened enamel. Rinsing with water and allowing saliva to act is preferable before brushing.

questions.prompt: Detecting and treating early cervical enamel demineralization after removal of orthodontic appliances is which level of prevention?
questions.explanation: Recognition and non-operative treatment of an early demineralized lesion aims to stop progression: secondary prevention. The original sentence describes a finding without naming an intervention.
questions.note: Repaired to explicitly state detection and treatment of an early lesion.

originalQuestion.prompt: The following example is related to which level of prevention? Adolescents with cervical demineralization of the teeth after removal of orthodontic appliances.

questions.prompt: Which of the following provides energy in the body?
questions.explanation: Amino acids can be oxidized for energy; vitamins facilitate metabolism but do not themselves provide dietary energy.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 29–32, 109–116 (PDF counter).

questions.prompt: Which age group has the highest need of protein per kg of body weight?
questions.explanation: Infants have the greatest conventional protein requirement per kilogram among these groups because of rapid growth. Total grams per day is a different comparison.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 111–115, 342–346 (PDF counter).
